title: A Note for His Mother
hookLine: a mother begs her son to come home; he answers on a scrap of paper
carry: karma or effort? first ask who the doer is
tomorrow: at sixteen, a healthy boy lies down as if dead. why?

lines: A PENCIL, A SCRAP OF PAPER.
cards: 1898, the hill at Tiruvannamalai. A woman finds the son who vanished from home two years before. He was sixteen when he left a note and took the train.
Now he's a thin young ascetic who hardly speaks. His mother, Alagammal, weeps and begs: come home. Day after day she asks.
He says nothing. At last someone hands him a pencil and paper, and he writes her an answer.

teach.h: THE NOTE: WHAT'S MEANT TO BE, WILL BE.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the note says: the Ordainer guides each soul by its karma. What's destined not to happen won't, however hard you try; what's destined to happen will, however you try to stop it.
So the best course is to stay silent. She went home. And there's Hinduism's old quarrel on one scrap of paper.

One side stresses karma already in motion, called prarabdha: seeds planted long ago, bearing fruit now. At its best, that view brings humility, and stops people blaming themselves for what they couldn't control.
The other side stresses effort: nothing grows without work, and the next step is still taken today. Decades later Ramana gave the quarrel one verse in his Forty Verses.

In paraphrase: the argument over which wins, fate or free will, belongs only to those who don't know the root of both. Know the self, the root of fate and effort alike, and you're free of both. Look at the move.
Both sides assume a doer in the middle, a karta, pushed by fate or pushing back. Ramana asks who that doer is.
Near the poem's end he says: if we're the doers, we taste the fruit; when, by asking who the doer is, the self is known, the sense of being the doer drops, and all three kinds of karma with it.
Many readers hear the note to his mother the same way: not a shrug, but a son who no longer took himself to be the one steering. And the story didn't end there.
Years later Alagammal came to live near him on the hill, and stayed for the rest of her life.

how: Hindus talk about karma and effort in daily life, at graduations and weddings alike; Ramana's followers bring the question back to 'who is the doer?'

games.q: the old quarrel — tap the pairs.

s: Ramana's verse says everything is fixed, so trying is pointless
it calls fate-versus-effort a quarrel for those who don't know the root of both.
his verse calls the self the root of fate and effort alike
knowing it, the verse says, frees one from both.
Ramana's mother went home and never saw him again
years later she came to live near him on the hill for the rest of her life.

games.q: you lean toward effort: work is what counts. what's the best case for the side that stresses fate?
o: it brings humility and stops you blaming yourself for what you couldn't control.
it means you never have to try at anything again.
it proves effort is fake and nobody really chooses.
games.why: both sides have a real strength. Ramana's verse doesn't crown either; it asks who the doer is.

practice: Do one small thing within reach: straighten a cup, close a drawer, fold the corner of a blanket. Do it slowly. For the rest of the sit, watch for the thought that says I did that, and ask, gently, who.

wordCard.voice: Ramana's Forty Verses: a poem that meets the fate-or-effort quarrel by asking who the doer is.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the doer; Ramana's verses ask who it is.

carryVoice: Pocket this: karma or effort? First ask who the doer is, the way Ramana's verse does. Rest well tonight.
